column2: The US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank aim for 2 % inflation over the medium term.
The Bank of Mexico targets 3 % inflation, with a margin of one point above or below.
In June 2022, US inflation reached 9.1 %, the highest in about 40 years.
Japan kept negative interest rates from 2016 to 2024.
In the early eighties, the Federal Reserve raised its rate to nearly 20 % to curb inflation of almost 15 %.
At 7 % compound interest a year, savings double in about 10 years: 72 divided by the rate gives the years (rule of 72).
In the United States, deposit insurance covers up to 250,000 dollars per person and per bank.
In Mexico, IPAB protects deposits up to 400,000 UDIS per person and per bank: about 3 million pesos.
In Mexico, personal income tax rises in brackets up to a rate of 35 %.
Mexico collects about 17 % of its GDP in taxes, the lowest share in the OECD.
OECD countries collect on average about a third of their GDP in taxes.
The United Arab Emirates does not charge personal income tax.
The standard VAT rate in Mexico is 16 %.
The UN has 193 member states.
In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote.
In Mexico the president serves a single 6-year term, with no re-election.
Japan's public debt is more than twice the size of its economy, the highest among rich countries.
The US Constitution, from 1787, is the oldest written constitution still in force.
World military spending reached about 2.7 trillion dollars in 2024, a record.
The United States accounts for about 37 % of the world's military spending.
Costa Rica abolished its army in 1948.
Nine countries have nuclear weapons.
Since 1945 no nuclear weapon has been used in a war.
About 6 in 10 workers in the world are in the informal economy.
In Mexico, more than half of employed people work informally.
In Mexico the minimum Christmas bonus by law is 15 days of wages.
About 2 in 10 new businesses in the United States close before their first year.
The 2026 World Cup is the first with 48 teams and three host countries.
Boxing has been an Olympic sport since 1904; it was only missing in Stockholm 1912.
Streaming generates about two thirds of global recorded music revenue.

Your country at a glance: GDP (the size of its economy), growth, stability, debt and relations. If you govern, this is where you change the system of government and form new nations.
Each province has population, wealth, happiness and development. Investing and building make them grow; occupied or very unhappy provinces can rebel.

Your armies: soldiers, quality (rises with spending per soldier), morale and supply. In war, time runs month by month: you move troops, fight and besiege provinces. Every extra soldier costs money from the treasury.
The budget splits the country's money among the army, research, welfare and more. High taxes raise more, but cut growth and approval; if you spend more than comes in, debt goes up.

Each country's opinion of you depends on its ideology, recent history and your actions. Alliances and pacts protect you, and allies join your wars with their armies. You have few diplomatic actions per year: use them where they matter most.

The war report sums up the war: occupied provinces, casualties and war weariness on each side. A country capitulates if it loses more than half its population or is exhausted; before that, peace is negotiated.
The ranking orders countries by score: 40 % economy (GDP), 30 % population and 30 % military power. Here you see your place and who is ahead.
The cabinet: the government's ministries, each with its head. A capable head improves the results of their area; directives change its priorities at a cost.

The system of government changes how fast your country grows, how much it researches, how many recruits it has and how much it collects. Changing it costs stability and is only possible every 4 years.
At the peace conference you spend peace points: each province costs 1, freeing a country 1 and reparations 2. If the enemy capitulated, you can take everything you occupy.

Purchasing power
What you can buy with your money. If prices rise faster than your income, your purchasing power falls even if you earn more.
Compound interest
Earning interest on interest already earned. At 7 % a year, savings double in about 10 years; with a debt it works the same way, but against you.
Price index
A number that tracks the cost of a basket of goods and services. If it goes from 1.00 to 1.10, prices rose 10 %.
Real rate
The interest rate minus inflation. It is what your savings really earn, or your debt really costs you, in purchasing power.
Central bank
The institution that issues a country's currency and sets its policy rate to keep inflation low and stable, like the Bank of Mexico or the Federal Reserve.
Policy rate
The rate set by the central bank. Raising it makes credit more expensive and curbs inflation; lowering it makes credit cheaper and boosts the economy.
Credit
Money a bank lends you in exchange for paying it back with interest in regular payments.
Investment fund
Money from many people that a manager invests in many stocks or bonds: you diversify without picking them one by one.
Bond
A loan you make to a government or a company: it pays you fixed interest and returns your money at maturity.
Return
What an investment earns over a period, as a % of what was invested: interest, dividends and price change.
Short selling
Betting that a price will fall: you sell borrowed shares and buy them back later. If the price rises, the loss has no limit.
Margin
Buying with money lent by your broker. It multiplies gains and losses alike.
Capital gain
What you earn by selling something for more than you paid. In many countries it is taxed.
Going public
When a company sells shares to the public for the first time to raise money and grow.
Recession
When a country's economy shrinks instead of growing: unemployment and bankruptcies rise.
Deflation
A general fall in prices. It sounds like good news, but it usually comes with lower sales, fewer jobs and heavier debts.
Hyperinflation
Runaway inflation, of 50 % or more per month: the currency loses its value within weeks.
Marginal rate
The tax percentage charged on the last dollar you earn: that of your highest bracket.
Effective rate
All the tax you pay divided by all your income. With a bracketed tax it is always lower than the marginal rate.
Progressive tax
A tax in brackets: each income bracket pays a higher rate, but only on the part that falls within that bracket.
Public debt
What the government owes. It is measured as a % of GDP; if it grows too much, interest eats up the budget and markets doubt it can pay.
Deficit
When the government spends more in a year than it collects. It is covered with debt or by printing money.
Budget
The government's spending plan for the year: how much goes to the army, education, health and everything else.
Exchange rate
How many units of your currency one dollar or another currency costs.
Devaluation
When your currency loses value against others: imports get more expensive and your exports get cheaper for other countries.
International reserves
Foreign currency and gold that the central bank holds to pay for imports and debts and to defend its currency.
Sanctions
Trade penalties from other countries: less trade and less growth for the sanctioned country.
Trade agreement
An agreement between countries to trade with fewer barriers: it usually raises growth for both.

Why
At this level there are no taxes or inflation.
In Realistic there are: here you would see how much you pay per bracket and how prices change what you can buy.
Taxes by bracket
With no income this year you pay no income tax.
Each rate applies only to the part of your income that falls within its bracket. That is why your effective rate is lower than your marginal rate, and earning more never leaves you with less money.
Prices and purchasing power
If your income rises less than inflation, you can buy less than last year even if you earn more.
Real interest rates
Real rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation: it is what your savings really earn, or your debt really costs you, in purchasing power.
With a positive real rate, saving pays and expensive credit cools the economy and prices.
With a negative real rate, saving loses purchasing power and borrowing is cheap: that pushes up spending and prices.

For your next life:
Opening an account while young lets compound interest do its work.
Spending less than you earn, even a little, is the basis of any net worth.
Investing part of your savings in a diversified fund usually beats inflation in the long run.
Starting a business is risky, but a well-run company can give you more than a salary.
Try another country or level: the same decisions give different results depending on the economy.
